hops.title: Why ordinary mice are less sensitive to diphtheria toxin
hops.text: Human cells are far more sensitive to diphtheria toxin than mouse cells are. The toxin has to dock onto a membrane-anchored growth factor, HB-EGF, before it can shut down protein synthesis, and amino acid substitutions in the mouse version spoil the fit. In 2001 Saito and colleagues put the human receptor into mouse liver cells; injected toxin damaged those cells, with no obvious abnormalities in other tissues in that experiment. Later work showed the toxin also reaches the central nervous system. Duan and colleagues expressed the receptor in genetically marked neurons; toxin depleted 82 percent of labelled lumbar dorsal-cord neurons and depleted labelled neurons in the hindbrain spinal trigeminal nucleus.

hops.title: Why nearby touch dulls pain more than distant touch
hops.text: Notice where your hand goes the instant you bang a shin on a coffee table: straight to the skin beside the bump, not to the other leg. Does it matter where the touch lands? Mancini and colleagues put light touches on either side of a painful laser pulse on volunteers' forearms, 1, 5 or 9 centimetres away. At 1 and 5 centimetres people had more trouble telling two pulse strengths apart and leaned toward the lower rating; at 9 centimetres that lean was not detected. In a separate hand experiment, nearby touch weakened a blink reflex generated in the brainstem, so some of the gating sits below the cortex.

sources.citation: Mancini F, Nash T, Iannetti GD, Haggard P. Pain. 2014;155(3):635-642. PMCID: PMC3988987.
Mancini F, Beaumont AL, Hu L, Haggard P, Iannetti GD. Pain. 2015;156(10):1936-1944. PMID: 26058037.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student sitting on a sofa gently rubbing one shin next to a wooden coffee table.
image.caption: Nearby touch biased pain ratings lower, with no clear shift at 9 centimetres; separately, nearby touch weakened a brainstem reflex.

hops.title: The substance-P blocker that prevents chemotherapy vomiting
hops.text: In the 1990s drug companies tested blockers of NK1r, the substance-P receptor carried by most mouse lumbar lamina I neurons traced from the lateral parabrachial area. In animals the blockers damped sensitized pain responses; in human pain trials the class disappointed. Substance P also acts in brainstem circuits involved in vomiting, and L-754,030 cut vomiting in ferrets. In a 1999 cisplatin trial where everyone received standard day-one antinausea drugs, 82 percent given L-754,030 before chemotherapy and through day five had neither vomiting nor retching on days two to five, versus 33 percent given placebo from day one through day five. It reached the clinic in 2003 as aprepitant.
